newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin spends weekend at Moscow clinic for checks.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin spends weekend at Moscow clinic for checks.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin will stay in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital for the weekend to allow doctors to carry out more tests ahead of forthcoming heart surgery, a Kremlin spokesman said.

He told Reuters there was nothing unusually wrong with the 65-year-old president, who returned from his holiday home near the capital on Thursday to begin a series of check-ups. It was simply easier for the doctors to work in the hospital, he said.

"This is not a situation created by an unforeseen event," the spokesman said. "There is no question of this being an emergency hospitalisation. It is the continuation of the planned checks since a number of tests and examinations can be effectively conducted only as an in-patient."

The spokesman did not say precisely when Yeltsin planned to leave. The president broke a long tradition of Kremlin silence on his health by announcing on September 5 that he would have heart surgery, probably at the end of September in Moscow.

His doctors said on Thursday after checks that they would meet again around September 28 to set the date of the operation, which they say will be a bypass to improve blood supply to the heart. Several foreign specialists are also being consulted.
The Central Clinical Hospital in western Moscow has long specialised in treatment for Soviet and now Russian leaders.

Yeltsin's wife Naina, whom he visited on Thursday, had a kidney operation there on August 24 and spokesmen have said she will remain in hospital until next week. The president said on September 5 she had suffered some minor complications.
Doctors have said Yeltsin needs a relatively simple bypass, in which a vein or artery is removed from one part of the body and grafted into the heart area to improve the flow of blood.

But the range of different types of bypass means that those outside the narrow group of doctors and officials involved in organising the operation are still in the dark as to the seriousness of his ailment and the risks involved. Apparent delay in carrying out the operation has added to the confusion.

Leo Bokeria, the director of one of Russia's leading heart clinics, said on Friday Yeltsin could be undergoing pre-surgical treatment. The weaker a patient's heart contractions the more pre-surgical treatment was needed and the more dangerous the operation. But the delay might only be for extra consultations.
Michael Rees, cardio-radiologist at Bristol Royal Infirmary in England, said a delay implied something had to be corrected.
He cited a variety of problems including diabetes, blood pressure or kidney problems. Or they could be weaning Yeltsin off a course of drugs, such as steroids.

Two top German cardiologists will join the Russian team of experts. Russian media have said pioneering U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey will also join the team. DeBakey said he had not been approached, but would be happy to help if asked to do so.
Yeltsin's absence has prompted speculation about who would take the reins when the president had his operation and who would hold the "red button" triggering Russia's nuclear arsenal.
